title: Products are part of services
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Products are part of services. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The repair booking page says a technician will arrive Tuesday. Tuesday passes without a visit. Was the page badly designed, or did the service behind it fail? The customer does not separate those questions. This lesson follows a product promise beyond the screen to the people, systems, and policies that must fulfill it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at what this moment reveals?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Most meaningful products sit inside a network of people, policies, operations, channels, and data. Service design looks across that network. It asks how a person moves through touchpoints and what backstage work makes the frontstage experience possible.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This shifts the design question from “How do we improve this screen?” to “What must work together for this person to get the outcome we promised?”

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Services are co-created over time. The customer brings needs, choices, information, effort, and expectations. Staff, systems, partners, policies, and physical environments respond. The product interface is a boundary object: it can coordinate the relationship well or make the complexity invisible until it fails.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we follow the mechanism step by step?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Service map: trace “Book a home repair” across the visible journey and the work beneath it.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: On the line: visible touchpoints—website, confirmation, live status, technician conversation, receipt.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Below the line: backstage elements—availability system, address data, technician dispatch, parts inventory, support policy.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Draw a red thread from an incorrect address in the booking flow to the failed visit. The lesson: a visible problem often begins somewhere else.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: How to read a service map

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A journey describes the person's steps, goals, questions, emotional highs and lows, and visible touchpoints. A service blueprint extends this by showing the line of interaction between customer and organisation, the frontstage actions visible to the person, and the backstage processes, systems, policies, and suppliers that enable them.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the map to locate dependencies and handoffs, not to create a decorative wall chart. Ask where information is created, copied, lost, or contradicted; who owns recovery when a promise breaks; which policy silently shapes the user experience; and whether staff have the information and authority needed to help.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Improvements should be tested across the full journey, especially around handovers and exceptions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The difference between a journey and a service

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A journey is seen through the customer's eyes. It is the sequence of events and touchpoints as they experience them, including what they are trying to do and how they feel at each point. A service is the system that makes that journey possible.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It includes visible interactions but also staffing, rules, data flows, technical integrations, capacity planning, procurement, and escalation paths.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This distinction helps a product designer know when to widen the room. If a screen repeatedly receives complaints, the best response may be an interface change. But if the screen is compensating for a late dispatch process, unclear policy, or missing staff authority, the cause belongs in the service.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Product teams become more credible when they can show the relationship rather than merely report that “the UI is broken.”

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design for the normal journey, then deliberately map the exceptions: no availability, missing data, changed mind, payment failure, late provider, disputed result, and escalation. The way a service handles these moments often determines whether the person trusts it afterwards.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Optimizing a single touchpoint while worsening the handoff to another team. Mapping only screens, not policies, staff, systems, and failure recovery. Assuming a status message fixes an operational problem. Forgetting that customers remember the broken promise, not the internal team boundary.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When a digital fix does not improve the journey, inspect the policy, staff workflow, data, or handoff that the interface is exposing rather than causing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners identify the owner and leverage point without claiming authority over every service function. They use blueprints to negotiate shared states, capacity, and recovery, then measure whether burden moved between channels. They treat a frontstage promise as an operational commitment with an accountable service owner.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A food-delivery app can present a perfect order tracker, but the experience depends on restaurant preparation, courier assignment, map accuracy, substitutions, refunds, and customer support. Interface design matters. So does the operational design that makes its promises true. When the service cannot meet its promise, clear and timely communication becomes part of the product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 4 made context part of the design. lesson 5 makes the system around the product visible, preparing the quality lens in lesson 6 and the later service-design module.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When an app tells you “Your order is delayed,” ask: What backstage decision or constraint is this interface translating, and does the message help me act on it?
